description:
Family team building Vowelstream, an Earth Jukebox: move a pointer over NASA Earth visualizations and hear the data. Move to explore, stop to listen.

I’m Dmytro: I think in functions; since middle school I’ve built complex Desmos visualizations. I turn math into sound and images: DSP, formant/modal synthesis (NumPy, C++), OpenCV, Python, NN, JS, ESP32.

Built a node-graph audio/image tool, an autonomous OpenCV robot that finds and pushes targets, and an Arduino fingerprint lock.
summary:
Vowelstream is a web app that lets you hear NASA Earth visualizations. You move a probe across a frame of NASA SVS 3912 (ECCO2 ocean currents and sea surface temperature) and the pixels under it become a voice in real time: temperature, read back from NASA's own colour scale, chooses a vowel (cold water says "oo", warm water opens to "ah"); the texture of the streaks shapes the voice; currents become stereo surf, land becomes wind; ring eddies are detected and heard as a pulse; 160 named places are spoken aloud.

Every sound is computed live from the data by a formant synthesizer in the browser: no recordings, no samples, no music. Keyboard-only control and screen-reader support make the same frames explorable without sight.

Not beeps, vowels: a voice can be listened to for hours, so the data can be studied, not just noticed.
details:
What it does
Vowelstream turns NASA Earth visualizations into sound you can explore. The input is a visualization frame or a looping video of NASA SVS 3912 — ECCO2 ocean currents and sea surface temperature — selectable from a source catalogue; the video is analysed live, frame by frame. A probe follows the pointer (or the arrow keys) across the map, and everything you hear is computed from the pixels under it: a vowel voice for temperature, stereo surf for currents, wind for land, a pulse for ring eddies, and spoken place names. There are no recordings and no samples; every sound is synthesized in the browser from the data.

How it works
1. Reading the data back. NASA's temperature colour bar is sampled into a lookup table and inverted by hue, so each streak pixel maps to °C (mean error about 0.2 °C against the source video). Grey pixels are classified as land, black gaps as no data. The probe reports the mean, the spread and separate left/right halves for stereo. Adding another EIC dataset means adding its colour scale and a file to the catalogue — still image or video.
2. A model of the vocal tract. The voice is a source–filter model: a harmonic source with amplitudes 1/n^1.6 (a glottal-like spectrum) drives three parallel second-order resonators at the formants F1, F2, F3 (bandwidths 60, 80, 100 Hz). Temperature moves the point along a vowel path in the F1–F2 plane (u → ɯ → y → i → ɛ → e → a) whose colours coincide with NASA's scale, and shifts the pitch half an octave. Loudness is equalized analytically from the filtered harmonic series, so a narrow "u" is not louder than an open "a".
3. Structure tensor of the streaks. Luma gradients over the probe give the 2×2 structure tensor; its eigen-direction is the flow axis and its coherence tells calm, parallel flow from tangled eddies. Coherence controls breathiness and jitter of the voice; the axis steers the surf between the ears.
4. Vortex detector. For a ring eddy the gradient is radial, so we measure the radial share of gradient energy in small disks at three radii, searched coarse-to-fine inside the probe, and confirm it with four quadrant tensors whose axes must run tangentially. A lock starts the pulsar: the wind layer is amplitude-modulated and rotated in stereo, from 3 Hz rising to 5 Hz over seven seconds.
5. Real-time audio in the browser. Getting this to run glitch-free took real engineering: we profiled the audio threads of Chrome and Firefox, found that custom-waveform oscillators rebuild their wavetables lazily on the audio thread (audible dropouts), and replaced them with precomputed looped buffers; per-frame image analysis runs under a CPU budget, sound parameters glide instead of stepping, and a built-in dropout meter compares the audio clock with the wall clock. The map wraps around the globe at the date line, and the surf uses pink noise shaped by a baked swell envelope.

Accessibility
Keyboard-first (any arrow key shows a blinking probe), spoken place names from a 160-entry gazetteer, temperature on demand, live-region status for screen readers, nothing plays until asked, automatic pause when the window is inactive.

Tools
Vanilla JavaScript ES modules, Web Audio API, Canvas 2D, Web Speech API; Python/NumPy and Pillow for calibration and detector validation on the frame; Firefox Profiler and Chrome DevTools for real-time audio debugging; nginx hosting. The landing-page illustrations, the characters and the presentation imagery are AI-generated — the ones you see are roughly the thirtieth attempt; the data, the sound and the code are not.

Why vowels
Tones near 1 kHz are tiring and sit where the ear is most sensitive. Vowels are decoded effortlessly since birth, so the data can be listened to for hours and compared across a map, not just noticed.

Team
Two people: sound, mathematics and vision (formant synthesis, detectors, the vowel idea) and architecture and delivery (data pipeline, engine integration, deployment).
dataRefs: Global Sea Surface Currents and Temperature
projectRefs: Peterson G., Barney H., «Control Methods Used in a Study of the Vowels», JASA 1952
